newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weakening yen brings Japan more pain than pleasure.
newsitem.headline: Weakening yen brings Japan more pain than pleasure.

text.p: By Linda Sieg, Chief Economics Correspondent Japan
Japanese officials and corporate executives who less than two years ago yelped with pain as the yen soared are now bemoaning its precipitous drop.
Why the change?

Behind the new complaints are a plethora of factors. These range from a rise in manufacturers' output overseas and corporate discomfort over wild currency swings that wreak havoc with long-term plans to worries that an ever-weaker yen might help trigger a "triple bear" scenario in which Japan's currency, shares and bond prices all collapse at once.

Japanese financial mandarins, who first showed signs of discomfort when the yen slid to 115 yen to the dollar last November, have been lamenting the currency's steep decline more loudly since the start of the year.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka voiced official concerns again on Tuesday, terming the yen's dive to 118 yen to the dollar "excessive" and promising Japan would take appropriate steps to combat wild currency moves.
On Wednesday, Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita said the weak yen had not spawned domestic inflation, but that he would watch closely to see if recent sharp currency moves affected the economy.

Part of the pressure to stem the yen's slide comes from big manufacturers, which have been shifting output offshore since the mid-1980s when the yen began its relentless climb against the dollar, analysts said.
"Industry has been screaming, saying at current (foreign exchange) levels, the money they invested overseas was wasted," said Mineko Sasaki-Smith, chief economist at CS First Boston.
The yen, now hovering around 118 yen to the dollar, is worth some 47 percent less against the greenback than in April 1995, when it hit its record high of 79.75 yen to the dollar.
Toyoda Motor Corp president Hiroshi Toyoda, for one, said earlier this month that an exchange rate between 100 and 110 yen would be best both for Japanese carmakers and U.S. rivals.
Business executives are also allergic to the sort of exchange rate volatility which can make nonsense out of long-term investment strategies.

"Some firms are distressed by a weak yen and others by a strong yen, but the majority view is that they all hate extreme and rapid changes in the exchange rate," said an executive at a big business organisation. "Investment plans have to be made looking 10 or 20 years ahead, but if the yen moves a lot in either direction, those plans have to be redone."
Officials also fear that what goes down sharply could go up just as steeply, raising prospects of a resurgent yen down the road, some economists said.

"Exchange rates often tend to overshoot...and what you get is a sudden bounce back either from an oversold or overbought level," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers. "Central banks don't like volatility and their job is to minimise it."

Shorter-term, some cite fears that an ever-weaker yen will spark a vicious cycle in which foreigners "sell Japan" by dumping stock and bond holdings, rather than watch the value of those assets decline further in home currencies, as a key element behind attempts at verbal intervention.

"The main worry is due to the 'triple-weakness' (scenario) of falling currency, stocks and bonds," one government source said. Tokyo share prices have slumped since late last year on concern over the economy and financial institutions' health.

Monetary authorities taking a considered view of the structural changes that Japan's economy must undergo to ensure future competitiveness are also loath to see the pressure exerted by a robust yen fade, economists say.

A strong yen boosts the cost of Japanese goods in dollar terms and thus makes exports less competitive. It also makes imports cheaper, putting Japanese firms on the defensive in their home market. Hence the cries of pain two years ago.

"If you look at the yen since the early 1970s, it has continually risen and that has been quite a force for structural change, encouraging cheaper imports...and making Japanese companies restructure costs to keep competitive," Jones said.
"In the last 18 months we've seen a sudden reversal of that, and concern is that the structural adjustment is now being discouraged," he said.
